objectives: Name the four lung volumes and four capacities, and explain why a spirometer cannot measure RV, FRC or TLC.
Read FEV1, FVC and the FEV1/FVC ratio off a spirogram, and the peak and downslope off a flow-volume loop.
Tell an obstructive pattern (asthma, emphysema) from a restrictive one (fibrosis) on the curves and the volume bars.
Predict how a bronchodilator and poor effort change the curves, and why poor effort can look like disease.

asthma.prompt: In asthma the airways narrow, so air meets more resistance on its way out. The lung itself is its usual size. What happens to FEV1 and to the FEV1/FVC ratio?
choices: FEV1 falls a lot, more than FVC, so the ratio falls
FEV1 and FVC fall together, so the ratio stays normal
FEV1 rises, because the lung holds more air
Nothing changes until the lung itself shrinks
asthma.why: Narrow airways slow the air down, so less of it gets out in the first second. Given time, most of the breath still leaves, so FVC falls far less than FEV1 and the ratio drops: the obstructive pattern.

emphysema.prompt: Emphysema destroys the walls between air sacs. The lung stretches easily but recoils weakly, so the chest wall's outward spring wins at a bigger size. What happens to the lung volumes?
choices: RV, FRC and TLC all rise: the lung is overinflated
Every volume falls, as in a stiff lung
Only the tidal volume rises
The volumes stay normal; only the flows change
emphysema.why: With weak recoil, the balance with the chest wall sits at a bigger volume, so FRC and TLC rise. Small airways collapse during the blow and trap air behind them, so RV rises most of all.

fibrosis.prompt: Scar tissue makes the lung stiff, so it recoils hard and cannot fill as far. The airways are open. What happens to the FEV1/FVC ratio?
choices: It stays normal or rises: FEV1 and FVC fall together
It falls, as it does in asthma
It drops close to zero
It cannot be measured in a stiff lung
fibrosis.why: A stiff lung is small, so both FEV1 and FVC fall. Its strong recoil empties it fast through open airways, so the share out in the first second stays normal or rises. That is why the ratio alone cannot show restriction: TLC has to be measured.

bronchodilator.prompt: This person has asthma. An inhaled bronchodilator relaxes the tightened airway muscle, and the test is repeated. Which part of the forced breath improves most?
choices: FEV1 and the peak: air gets out faster
TLC: the lung grows larger
RV rises as the airways open
Nothing: the forced breath is the same as before
bronchodilator.why: Wider airways let air out faster, so FEV1 and the peak rise and less air stays trapped. The lung's size does not change. A large enough rise in FEV1 or FVC is a significant bronchodilator response.

effort.prompt: A healthy lung, but the person starts the blow slowly and stops early. What happens to the curves and to the lung volumes?
choices: The curves fall; the lung volumes stay the same
The curves and the lung volumes both fall
The curves stay normal; TLC falls
The curves rise, because the blow lasts longer
effort.why: A weak start lowers the peak and a short blow cuts FVC, so the curves can look like disease. But the lung is unchanged, so RV, FRC and TLC are the same. The test is coached and repeated.

quiz.stem: Why can a spirometer not measure residual volume?
choices: Residual air never leaves the lungs, so it never passes the mouthpiece
Residual air leaves too fast for the spirometer to record
Residual volume is only present during a forced breath
The spirometer only records air breathed in
quiz.why: A spirometer sees only air that moves through it. Residual air stays in even after the hardest breath out, so RV, and FRC and TLC which contain it, need a body box or a gas test.

quiz.stem: Which volumes add up to vital capacity?
choices: IRV, TV and ERV
TV, ERV and RV
IRV and RV only
All four volumes, including RV
quiz.why: Vital capacity is all the air you can move: both reserves plus the tidal breath. Adding RV as well gives total lung capacity, the tempting wrong answer.

quiz.stem: What sets the volume of air left in the lungs at the end of a quiet breath out (FRC)?
choices: The balance between the lung's inward recoil and the chest wall's outward spring
The strongest breath out a person can make
How much air the airways can hold
The size of the last tidal breath
quiz.why: At FRC no muscle is working: the lung pulls in and the chest wall springs out, equally. A lung with weak recoil (emphysema) settles bigger; a stiff one (fibrosis) settles smaller.

quiz.stem: What does the FEV1/FVC ratio tell you?
choices: The share of the forced breath that leaves in the first second
How much air is left in the lungs after the blow
The total size of the lungs
How fast air flows in when breathing in
quiz.why: The ratio is about speed of emptying, not size. A small lung can have a normal ratio, which is why a low TLC, not the ratio, shows restriction.

quiz.stem: Blowing harder raises the peak of a flow-volume loop, but not its downslope. Why?
choices: The squeeze that pushes air out also narrows the airways, so flow is set by recoil and airway width
The lungs run out of air before the peak
Effort only acts during breathing in
The spirometer cannot record flows above the peak
quiz.why: Past the peak, more chest pressure also presses on the airways, so flow stops rising with effort. That makes the downslope a fair picture of the lung and its airways, and poor effort shows mainly in the peak and the length of the blow.

quiz.stem: A test shows a low FEV1/FVC ratio, a scooped downslope, a normal TLC and a slightly raised RV. Which fits best?
choices: An obstructive pattern, as in asthma
A restrictive pattern, as in fibrosis
Poor effort with a healthy lung
A normal test
quiz.why: A low ratio means slow emptying: obstruction. Narrow airways trap a little air, so RV rises, while TLC stays normal. Fibrosis would lower TLC with a normal or high ratio.

quiz.stem: Why are TLC, FRC and RV all high in emphysema?
choices: The lung recoils weakly, so it settles bigger, and collapsing small airways trap air
Scar tissue makes the lung stiffer
The airway muscle tightens and swells
The chest wall becomes weaker than the lung
quiz.why: Destroyed air-sac walls mean weak recoil, so the balance with the chest wall sits at a bigger volume, and small airways that lost their support collapse during the blow, trapping air. Tightened, swollen airways describe asthma.

quiz.stem: A person with pulmonary fibrosis has a low FVC and a normal FEV1/FVC ratio. Which measurement confirms a restrictive pattern?
choices: A low TLC, measured with a body box or a gas test
A low FEV1/FVC ratio
A rise in FEV1 after a bronchodilator
A high peak expiratory flow
quiz.why: A low FVC can come from a small lung, trapped air or a short blow. Only a measured low TLC shows the lung is small. A spirometer cannot measure TLC, because TLC contains RV.

quiz.stem: After a bronchodilator, a person's FEV1 rises by more than the guideline's threshold for a significant response. What does this show?
choices: Airway narrowing that eases with treatment: it supports asthma but does not prove it alone
The person definitely has asthma and not COPD
The person has a restrictive lung disease
The first test was done with poor effort
quiz.why: A significant response shows narrowing that reverses. It fits asthma, but people with COPD can respond too and some with asthma do not, so the result is read alongside the whole picture.

quiz.stem: A test shows a low FVC and a low, late, rounded peak, and the person's blows do not agree with each other. What is the best next step?
choices: Coach the person and repeat until good blows agree
Report a restrictive pattern
Report an obstructive pattern
Give a bronchodilator and use the better curve
quiz.why: A rounded, late peak and blows that disagree point to poor effort, which can look like disease. Effort and repeatability are checked before any pattern is named.

takeaways: A spirometer sees only the air that moves: TV, IRV, ERV and the capacities built from them. RV, and FRC and TLC which contain it, need a body box or a gas test.
FRC is where the lung's inward recoil balances the chest wall's outward spring; weak recoil (emphysema) settles bigger, a stiff lung (fibrosis) smaller.
A forced blow gives FVC (all of it) and FEV1 (the first second). FEV1/FVC is the share out in the first second, judged against the person's lower limit of normal.
On the flow-volume loop, effort sets the peak, but the downslope is set by the lung's recoil and airways.
Obstruction (asthma, emphysema): FEV1 falls more than FVC, the ratio is low and the loop scoops; trapped air raises RV, and emphysema raises FRC and TLC too.
Restriction (fibrosis): every volume falls, FEV1 and FVC fall together, and the ratio is normal or high. Only a low TLC proves it.
A bronchodilator can raise FEV1 when narrowing reverses; a significant response supports asthma but does not diagnose it alone.
Poor effort lowers the curves without changing the lung: check that repeated good blows agree before naming any pattern.
